topics: 🔥 A Base for a Forbidden Object — even Rabbi Shimon agrees a burning lamp cannot be moved
🪔 Rebbi's Coal Pan Ruling — Rabbi Romanus's report and Abaye's chain of objections
🪑 Reassembling a Collapsible Loom or Bed — Torah liability, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's leniency
💧 Catching Sparks but Not Water — the mishna's fine line, and Rav Ashi's final reason

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Bases, Broken Vessels, and Beginning to Insulate
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 47a–47b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by confirming that even Rabbi Shimon agrees a lamp, oil, and wick become a 'base for a prohibited object' while lit, so none of it may be moved. Rabbi Romanus then reports that Rebbi permitted him to carry an ash-filled coal pan, prompting a long chain of objections from Abaye about what small residue (frankincense, broken sticks) can render a vessel movable, resolved through Rava's comparison to ashes usable for covering filth. The Gemara turns to reassembling collapsible objects like a weaver's loom, asking when doing so incurs a sin-offering, and resolves the question through Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's leniency for loosely-joined pieces. Perek Kira closes with the mishna about catching lamp sparks (but never adding water) and opens a new mishna, and chapter, on which materials may insulate a pot of food before Shabbat.

slides.title: 🔥 A Base for a Forbidden Object
slides.label: The opening principle:
slides.text: Leave the candle, oil, and wick as they are, since while lit they have become a base for a prohibited object (basis l'davar ha'asur). Even Rabbi Shimon, who is generally lenient about set-aside, agrees that a burning flame on Shabbat may not be moved — and so neither may anything supporting it.
slides.hebrewSource: הַנַּח לְנֵר שֶׁמֶן וּפְתִילָה, הוֹאִיל דְּנַעֲשָׂה בָּסִיס לַדָּבָר הָאָסוּר

slides.title: 🪔 Rebbi's Coal Pan: A Chain of Objections
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Romanus reports a leniency, and Abaye keeps pressing to explain it

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Romanus: Rebbi permitted me to carry a coal pan full of its ashes
2️⃣ Objection: compare to carrying a child holding a stone, or a basket of fruit with a stone inside — permitted only because of the fruit. What in the pan makes it permitted?
3️⃣ First answer: bits of unburned frankincense inside — rejected by Abaye, since such tiny bits in Rebbi's house were not significant enough to matter
4️⃣ Rava's final answer: the ashes themselves are usable to cover filth, so the pan is movable on their account — even broken sticks resting on it are nullified by the ashes

callout.label: One more distinction:
callout.text: A baraita that broken wick fragments make a lamp unmovable is explained as taught specifically in the Galilee, where oil was so cheap that broken wicks were never nullified relative to it.

slides.title: 🪑 Reassembling Collapsible Objects
slides.subtitle: When does putting pieces back together count as forbidden building?

boxes.title: Liable (chayav chatat)
items: Reassembling a weaver's loom — Rav and Shmuel
A round horn (complex to assemble) — Rabbi Simai

boxes.title: Exempt but forbidden
items: Bed frame, bed legs, or archer's tablets — if forced together

boxes.title: Fully permitted
items: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: if the pieces fit loosely, with ease — permitted even ab initio
A straight horn (simple to assemble) — Rabbi Simai

callout.label: Resolving the tension:
callout.text: Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiyya relied on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's leniency; Rava applied the same logic to his own family's collapsible bed.

slides.title: 💧 Sparks May Be Caught, Water May Not
slides.subtitle: The mishna's rule, tested against Rabbi Yosei's principle of indirect causation

nodes.content: 📜 Mishna: place a vessel to catch sparks from a lamp (fine — sparks have no substance), but do not add water to it, since that extinguishes them
❓ Is this the unattributed view of Rabbi Yosei, who forbids even indirectly causing something to be extinguished?
🚫 Rejected: a baraita states the same rule applies even on Shabbat eve — but Rabbi Yosei's concern is a Shabbat-only issue!
✅ Rav Ashi's answer: even the Rabbis (who normally permit indirect causes) forbid this, since placing water there hastens the extinguishing rather than merely causing it eventually

slides.title: 🥘 Opening a New Topic: Insulating a Pot
slides.subtitle: The new mishna (start of a new chapter) lists forbidden and conditionally-forbidden materials
rows: Pressed olive pulp (gefet), manure, salt, lime, sand
Forbidden whether moist or dry — they generate their own heat
Straw, grape pulp, soft rags (mochin), grass
Olive pulp raises heat and is always forbidden even to rest food upon; sesame pulp does not

summary.principle: A lamp still burning is a base for a forbidden object and may never be moved, small residues can render a vessel usable only if they carry genuine significance, and the mishna now turns to a new subject — which materials may insulate Shabbat's food without adding forbidden heat.

flowSteps.content: 🔥 A lit lamp is a base for a forbidden object — off-limits even to Rabbi Shimon
🪔 Rebbi's coal pan: movable because of usable ashes, not insignificant scraps

columns.content: 🪑 Reassembling loose-fitting pieces is permitted; forcing tight joints is not
💧 Catching sparks is fine; adding water hastens their extinguishing

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: a vessel's movability depends on whether what's attached to it truly has value — and a new chapter now asks the same of insulating materials

quiz.q: Why does even Rabbi Shimon, who is generally lenient about set-aside, agree that a burning lamp with its oil and wick may not be moved on Shabbat?
o: Lamps are always forbidden to touch
It has become a base for a prohibited object (basis l'davar ha'asur) since the flame itself may not be moved
Only priests may move lamps
The oil evaporates too quickly
quiz.e: The text states that once the lamp, oil, and wick support an active flame, they become a base for something prohibited, and even Rabbi Shimon agrees this cannot be moved.

quiz.q: According to Rava's final explanation, why may Rebbi's ash-filled coal pan be carried on Shabbat?
o: Because it contains valuable frankincense bits
The ashes themselves are usable for covering filth, which renders the whole pan movable, even with insignificant broken sticks resting in it
Because it belonged to Rebbi personally
Coal pans are never subject to set-aside
quiz.e: Rava explained that ashes have a genuine use — covering filth — so the pan is movable on their account, unlike Abaye's earlier proposal about insignificant frankincense fragments.

quiz.q: According to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, when is reassembling a collapsible object like a bed frame or loom permitted even ab initio?
o: Never — all reassembly is forbidden
When the pieces fit together loosely and easily, without being forced
Only if done before Shabbat begins
Only for religious objects
quiz.e: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's leniency, which Rabbi Abba, Rav Huna bar Chiyya, and Rava all relied upon, permits reassembly when the pieces are loose and go together with ease.

quiz.q: Why does Rav Ashi conclude that one may not add water to a vessel catching sparks, even according to the Rabbis who otherwise permit indirectly causing extinguishing?
o: Water is always forbidden near a flame
Adding the water hastens the extinguishing rather than merely being an indirect eventual cause
Only Rabbi Yosei's view matters here
The mishna does not actually forbid this
quiz.e: Rav Ashi distinguishes this case: placing water there actively speeds up the extinguishing of the sparks, which even the generally lenient Rabbis would prohibit.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna that opens on this daf, what distinguishes materials like salt, lime, and sand from materials like straw and grass regarding insulating a pot?
o: There is no difference between them
Salt, lime, and sand are forbidden whether moist or dry, since they generate their own heat, while straw and grass are forbidden only when moist
Straw and grass are always forbidden entirely
Salt and sand may only be used on Shabbat eve
quiz.e: The mishna forbids gefet, manure, salt, lime, and sand in any state because they generate heat, while straw, grape pulp, soft rags, and grass are forbidden only while moist and become permitted once dry.
